 From Ireland to Big Rapids: Eoin O'Sullivan making major impact on top-ranked Ferris
 State football team
 BIG RAPIDS, Mich. —  
 Growing up in Ireland , Eoin O'Sullivan developed his kicking skills playing a different kind of football than the one he
 now plays for the nationally top-ranked Ferris State Bulldogs.
 But those early experiences have helped prepare the sophomore kicker and punter for
 some of the biggest moments of his football career, including pressure-filled field
 goals in key victories over nationally ranked opponents this fall.
 "I grew up playing Gaelic football, which is the national sport of Ireland. It's a
 bit like soccer, but with your hands, and it involves a lot of kicking. That's kind
 of how I developed my kicking ability," O'Sullivan said. "I grew up loving American
 football as well. I started watching when I was probably 12 or 13 years old, so I
 always had it in my mind."
 Ferris State opens the 2026 NCAA Division II playoffs at home on Saturday, Nov. 21,
 hosting Truman State University at 12-noon at Top Taggart Field. The game has taken
 on added national significance with the announcement that FOX Big Noon Kickoff Show
 is coming to Big Rapids for its show from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. at the stadium.
 O'Sullivan joined Ferris State's football program ahead of the 2026 season after beginning
 his collegiate playing career at Roosevelt University, a fellow Great Lakes Intercollegiate
 Athletic Conference member.
 His journey to the United States began with an opportunity to turn his kicking ability
 into a college football scholarship.
 "I met a guy in Ireland who helps guys get scholarships to play American football,"
 O'Sullivan said. "I was training with him for about a year or a year and a half, and
 eventually, last summer, I got an offer from Roosevelt. It was a no-brainer."
 O'Sullivan embraced the challenge of learning a new sport while adjusting to college
 football in the United States, an experience that eventually led him to Ferris State
 head coach Tony Annese.
 "I played a year there and had a pretty good season," he said. "I entered the portal
 after the season, and Coach Annese hit me up."
 With the opportunity to join a Ferris State program that won back-to-back NCAA Division
 II national championships in 2024 and 2025 and four of the previous five, the decision
 was easy.
 "Who wouldn't want to play for the national champions?" O'Sullivan said.
 O'Sullivan credits the experience at Roosevelt with providing a foundation for his
 success at Ferris State.
 "I've got a lot of appreciation for the guys at Roosevelt for giving me that opportunity
 because, if it wasn't for them, I probably wouldn't have ended up here,” he said.
 “I really enjoyed my season there. I learned a lot about what it takes to be a football
 player because I'd never played football before."
 Learning the fundamentals of American football, particularly at the collegiate level,
 required a significant adjustment.
 "They really helped me understand the game, how to conduct yourself day to day, and
 I think that set me up really well for coming to Ferris," he said.
 O'Sullivan arrived at an important time for the Bulldogs, who entered the season facing
 graduation losses and injuries among their kickers and punters.
 He has since emerged as a valuable contributor to Ferris State's special teams, delivering
 in some of the Bulldogs' biggest games of the 2026 regular season.
 During Ferris State's 41-34 road victory over rival Grand Valley State University,
 O'Sullivan converted a 45-yard field goal before nearly 17,000 fans at Lubbers Stadium.
 It was a moment he won't soon forget, even if he doesn't remember much about the kick
 itself.
 "I think that's what you call a baptism of fire," O'Sullivan said. "I'd never kicked
 a field goal in my life, and then they sent me out there at Lubbers Stadium with the
 game tied. It's nice that ‘TA’ has that faith in me to hit those kicks."
 In a tight game played on a national stage and in front of a large rivalry crowd,
 O'Sullivan relied on preparation and instincts.
 "I don't remember the kick. I kind of blacked out," he said. "But I remember seeing
 the ball go through the uprights, and the relief — I don't think I've ever felt relief
 like that in my life."
 The experience provided a confidence boost for the specialist, who would soon be called
 upon again.
 One week later, O'Sullivan delivered another clutch kick, connecting on a 50-yard
 field goal in the third quarter of Ferris State's hard-fought 27-20 home victory over
 nationally ranked Michigan Tech.
 "I think it was a seven-point game at the time, and there were five seconds left in
 the quarter," he recalled. "I was relieved that (the coaches) got me in there in the
 third quarter because there was a pretty strong wind blowing at my back for that one."
 The kick brought back memories of his first field goal against GVSU.
 "Same as the Grand Valley one, I kind of blacked out, but I saw the ball going through
 the uprights," he said. "It's nice that they have that faith in me to hit those long
 ones, and hopefully I'll get another opportunity or two to do that this year."
 O'Sullivan (#45) surrounded with teammates during this year's Senior Day celebration.
 His performances earned him GLIAC Special Teams Player of the Week honors in consecutive
 weeks, but O'Sullivan was quick to share the recognition with his teammates.
 "It's not an individual award, that's for sure," he said. "We've got guys on this
 team who just want to win, and that shows on punt, on kickoff and on field goals.
 The protection unit on our field goals — I never have to worry about a kick being
 blocked. I never have to worry about a bad hold or a bad snap."
 O'Sullivan praised fellow kickers Jay Cady and Eddie Jewett , long snappers Brendan O'Brien and Derek Baxter , and versatile holder Leeshaun Mumpfield , among others, for their contributions to the Bulldogs' special-teams success.
 He also credited special teams coach Mike Palko for his dedication to the group.
 "He's a great guy to have around," said O'Sullivan, who has 17 punts with an average
 of 757 and a long of 61 yards. "He works long hours at night and then comes to practice
 in the morning, so he really dedicates a lot to Ferris State."
 Beyond individual accomplishments, O'Sullivan has embraced the winning culture of
 a Ferris State program that has established itself among the nation's elite.
 "I see that in the weight room. I see it on the field, with guys getting to the practice
 field an hour early," he said. "I think that's what sets this program apart from a
 lot of other programs — just that desire to win."
 O'Sullivan has also enjoyed competing in front of the Bulldog faithful.
 "The fans have been showing up these past few weeks, and obviously the weather's been
 nice, so that helps," he said. "It's a lot of fun playing at Top Taggart Field. The
 crowd really gets behind us. We hear them, and we really appreciate their support."
 His family has also had a chance to share in the experience.
 O'Sullivan's parents traveled from Ireland, and they witnessed both of his memorable
 field goals.
 "My parents chose two good games to come to," he said. "They came for the Grand Valley
 game and the Michigan Tech game, so they must be my lucky charm!"
 Now, O'Sullivan and his teammates have their sights set on an even bigger goal.
 The Bulldogs completed an undefeated regular season at 11-0, establishing a new NCAA
 Division II record with 41 consecutive victories and capturing their third straight
 GLIAC championship with a 63-20 win over O'Sullivan's former team, Roosevelt, on Saturday,
 Nov. 14.
 For O'Sullivan, who will be a big part of the environment on the field, the journey
 from Gaelic football in Ireland to championship football in Big Rapids has been unexpected
 but rewarding. And as the Bulldogs prepare for another postseason run, the young kicker
 hopes there are still more big moments ahead.
 "Confidence is definitely building with those two kicks," he said. "So long may it
 continue."
